background.definition: Acute disruption of the achilles tendon occurring most commonly in men between the ages of 30 and 50 years often resulting from sudden forced plantar flexion of the foot, unexpected dorsiflexion of the foot, or violent dorsiflexion of a plantar flexed foot.

list.listitem: A single study of incidence in Finland found the incidence rising from 2/100,000 per year in the early 1980s to 12/100,000 per year in the early 1990s.
The same study found that the peak age was between the ages of 30 and 39 years, with a male to female ratio of 5.5:1 and over 80% occurring during sports.
Advancing age
Chronic tendonopathies
Oral and/or local corticosteroids
Autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus or rheumatoid arthritis
Fluoroquinolone antibiotics
Mechanical abnormalities of the foot
Exercise-induced hyperthermia
It is generally accepted that ruptures usually occur in previously abnormal tendons.
The poorest blood supply to the tendon is approximately 2 to 6 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion and is most vulnerable to injury.
Poor blood supply, coupled with age-associated changes such as decreased cell density, decreased collagen fibril density, and loss of fiber waviness, predisposes the tendon to injury.

A positive Thompson (calf squeeze) test is highly suggestive of achilles tendon rupture in the patient who presents with the acute onset of posterior heel pain and an appropriate mechanism of injury. C
Delayed presentation may necessitate the use of plain films of the lateral ankle, ultrasound, or MRI to establish the diagnosis. C
The ability to plantar flex the foot does not rule out the diagnosis of achilles tendon rupture due to activity of accessory muscles. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Gradual onset; tendon intact to palpation; retained full strength with plantar flexion
Insidious onset; tender, palpable bursa; Haglund deformity often seen on plain film
Tendon intact to palpation; pain often anterior to lateral malleolus with typical injury
Swelling and/or defect more proximal; negative squeeze test

list.listitem: A diagnosis of achilles tendon rupture should be suspected in any patient who presents with acute posterior heel pain and decreased plantar flexion strength, especially if preceded by a sudden accelerative or jumping movement.
The patient will often report feeling or hearing a "pop" at the back of the heel at the time of injury.

Examination for suspected achilles tendon rupture should include the Thompson or “calf squeeze” test (squeezing calf results in no or minimal plantar flexion) and palpation of the tendon for a discernible gap.
The ability to actively plantar flex does not rule out the diagnosis of achilles tendon rupture due to action of the tibialis posterior, plantaris, and peroneal muscles.
Diagnostic radiologic studies are used infrequently and only when physical examination findings are equivocal or when a partial tear is suspected.

Soft tissue lateral plain film of the ankle should include evaluation of Kager’s triangle, whose borders are formed by deep flexor tendons anteriorly, the achilles tendon posteriorly, and the calcaneus inferiorly.
Partial opacification and loss of total area of Kager’s triangle suggest achilles tendon rupture; one study found that this finding in 60 of 60 achilles tendon ruptures proven at time of surgery.

Ultrasound and MRI are definitive studies but not often employed due to the ability to diagnose most ruptures on physical examination, as well as availability, cost, and/or technician experience considerations.
No relevant clinical decision rules are found.
Diagnosis is usually made by a careful history and physical examination; radiologic studies are rarely needed.
Patients with a delayed presentation (after 4 weeks) may benefit from radiologic studies if the diagnosis is equivocal due to hematoma formation and partial reconstitution of the tendon.
Operative versus nonoperative treatment remains controversial; however, clinical and functional outcomes are equal in the absence of significant complications. A
Operative treatment may result in a lower rate of rerupture but has a higher rate of complications; complications may be reduced by using a minimally invasive or a percutaneous surgical approach. B
Both types of management favor an early functional approach to rehabilitation over prolonged immobilization. B
Several surgical options exist, including open, minimally invasive, and percutaneous repair.

Clinical and functional outcomes are essentially the same regardless of the technique; however, postoperative complications are higher for the open procedure than minimally invasive or percutaneous treatments.

Surgery is generally accepted to have a lower rate of rerupture than nonoperative management (1.7%-3.5% vs 12.0%-20.8%, respectively). However, long-term (mean 15.7 years) follow-up of a RCT comparing operative to nonoperative management found no difference in re-rupture rates.

A 2022 Norwegian RCT randomized 554 adults age 18 to 60 with acute Achilles tendon rupture to non-operative management, open repair, and minimally invasive surgery. The nonoperative management involved a below-the-knee equinus cast for 2 weeks, followed by 6 weeks of weight-bearing as tolerated with heel wedges and ankle-foot orthoses. Patients had gradually decreasing plantar flexion with progressive removal of heel lifts in the 6 weeks following the equinus cast. The brace was worn day and night for the first 2 weeks but was removed at night for weeks 2 through 6. At 1 year, there was no difference in the primary outcome of a change in the Achilles tendon Total Rupture Score compared with baseline status pre-injury: -17 points for nonoperative treatment, -16 points for open repair, and - 14.7 points for minimally invasive surgery. Nerve injuries were less common with nonoperative management (0.6% vs 2.8% with open repair and 5.2% with minimally invasive surgery). However, re-ruptures were more common with nonoperative management (6.2% vs 0.6% in each of the surgery groups, number needed to treat to harm = 18), with most occurring in the 10 weeks following the index injury.
Postoperative rehabilitation favors early functional protocols over immobilization.
Nonoperative management was the standard of care prior to the institution of surgical therapy and remains a viable option.
Options range from prolonged cast immobilization to limited nonweight bearing with early functional rehabilitation; current trends are toward some form of early functional treatment.

In a United Kingdom multicenter RCT (n = 274) of nonoperative management, 8 weeks of below-knee plaster casts or functional braces (both followed by the same rehabilitation program) had equivalent outcomes after 9 months.A similar RCT (n = 140) comparing plaster casts to a walking boot found equivalent outcomes after 12 months.
Functional rehabilitation may include the use of a limited motion walking boot, early weight bearing, and physical therapy for range of motion and strengthening.
Platelet-rich plasma injections are no better than placebo injections at improving pain or functional outcomes.

This was also the conclusion of a trial randomizing 230 patients with acute complete Achilles tendon rupture to PRP or dry needle insertion. At the end of the study pain and function were similar between groups.
Some recent data suggest that nonoperative management with early functional protocols may yield rerupture rates approaching those of surgical repair.
Regardless of the form of management, postinjury rehabilitation often follows similar courses.
Limited or nonweight bearing is employed early and varies in duration depending on the aggressiveness of functional rehabilitation.
Functional and physical therapy protocols last for several weeks, and full recovery may take 6 to 12 months.
Most patients with achilles tendon rupture should be referred to an orthopedic surgeon for evaluation of operative versus nonoperative treatment.

Complications, other than rerupture, occur with both operative and nonoperative management; operative management produces a higher risk for complications (20%-35% for all types) than nonoperative management (2.5%-8%).
Common operative complications include delayed wound healing, granuloma, wound infection, nerve injury, and adhesions.
Nonoperative complications include tendon lengthening, nerve injury, and adhesions.
Deep venous thrombosis and chronic pain are seen in either form of management.

In the absence of significant complications, operative and nonoperative management approaches produce equal functional and clinical outcomes.
B

Most patients will return to preinjury levels of work or sports participation by 6 to 12 months, although some patients do not regain preinjury calf strength or do not participate in sports because of fear of rerupture.
B
Spontaneous rupture may occur in the elderly.
Treatment is generally nonoperative because of the risk of surgical complications and comorbidities.
